8. Data in and out, occurrence cleaning, web maps and recipes

guide-08-data-webmaps-recipes.Rmd
library(tidymapr)
library(dplyr)

1. Reading data

The concept

Spatial data come in two kinds (Chapter 1): vector data (points, lines, polygons with attribute tables) and raster data (grids of cells). tidymapr reads both through GDAL, the library behind QGIS, ArcGIS and GeoSpaX, so almost any format works. Every file must carry, or be given, its coordinate reference system (Chapter 2).

Data Common formats Read with Returns
Vector GeoPackage (.gpkg), shapefile (.shp), GeoJSON, KML, GPX geo_read() sf table
CAD drawings AutoCAD DXF geo_read(cad_layer = ) sf table
Raster GeoTIFF, ASCII grid, JPEG2000 geo_raster_read() SpatRaster
Multidimensional netCDF (.nc), HDF4, HDF5 (climate, satellite products) geo_raster_read(var = ) SpatRaster with one layer per time or depth
Tables CSV, Excel with coordinates read.csv(), then geo_as_sf() sf table 
# A file can hold several layers: list them first
geo_layers(system.file("shapes/world.gpkg", package = "spData"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   layer geometry      features fields
#>   <chr> <chr>            <int>  <int>
#> 1 world Multi Polygon      177     10

cantons <- geo_read(system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra"))
cantons

netCDF files from climate models and reanalyses hold many variables and time steps in one file:

era5 <- geo_raster_read(system.file("ex/nouragues.nc", package = "terra"))
era5
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 3, 3, 336  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.1005001, 0.0999999  (x, y)
#> extent      : -52.90525, -52.60375, 3.911, 4.211  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (CRS84) (OGC:CRS84)
#> sources     : nouragues.nc
#> varnames    : d2m (2 metre dewpoint temperature)
#>               sp (Surface pressure)
#>               ssrd (Surface solar radiation downwards)
#>               t2m (2 metre temperature)
#>               tp (Total precipitation)
#>               ...
#> names       : d2m_e~r=1_1, d2m_e~r=1_2, d2m_e~r=1_3, d2m_e~r=1_4, d2m_e~r=1_5, d2m_e~r=1_6, ...
#> unit        :           K,           K,           K,           K,           K,           K, ...
#> depth       : 1 to 5 (: 2 steps)
#> time        : 2021-01-01 00:00:00zUTC to 2022-12-01 00:00:00zUTC (24 steps)

How to read this. The file holds ERA5 climate reanalysis for the Nouragues station in French Guiana: 336 layers, made of several variables (dewpoint d2m, temperature t2m, precipitation tp, …) for each month of 2021-2022. Pick one with geo_raster_read(path, var = "t2m"); units are kelvin for temperature, as the unit line shows.

Coordinates in a spreadsheet 

sites <- read.csv("data/sites.csv")                 # columns lon, lat
sites <- geo_as_sf(sites, lon, lat)                 # WGS84 longitude/latitude

utm <- read.csv("data/plots_utm.csv")               # columns x, y in metres
utm <- geo_as_sf(utm, x, y, crs = 32755)            # say which UTM zone

tidymapr refuses coordinate columns that cannot be longitude and latitude unless you give their CRS, because treating metres as degrees would silently give wrong distances.

Writing 

geo_write(cantons, "output/cantons.gpkg")           # GeoPackage: the best general format
geo_write(cantons, "output/cantons.shp")            # shapefile, for older software
terra::writeRaster(era5[[1]], "output/d2m.tif")     # GeoTIFF

Prefer GeoPackage over shapefiles: one file instead of five, no 10-character limit on column names, and no 2 GB size limit.

2. Occurrence records from GBIF

The concept

The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) aggregates over two billion species records from museums, surveys and citizen science. They are invaluable and imperfect: coordinate errors are common, and they bias species distribution models (Chapter 5). Typical errors:

Error Example Test in geo_clean()
Zero coordinates 0°, 0° in the Gulf of Guinea "zeros"
Equal coordinates Longitude = latitude, a typing error "equal"
Country capitals and centroids The record was georeferenced to the country, not the site "capitals", "centroids"
Biodiversity institutions A museum’s own coordinates instead of the collecting site "institutions"
The GBIF headquarters Copenhagen "gbif"
Duplicates The same record from two datasets "duplicates"
Outliers Far from all other records of the species "outliers"

These follow CoordinateCleaner (Zizka et al. 2019), with the same default distances. The zero, equal-coordinate and GBIF tests give exactly CoordinateCleaner’s flags, which is checked in tidymapr’s tests; the capital and centroid tests use all 215 national capitals and three definitions of each country’s centroid from Natural Earth.

Download with geo_gbif("Oecophylla smaragdina", country = "PG") (needs internet). The records of the weaver ant Oecophylla smaragdina in Papua New Guinea are shipped with tidymapr, so this example runs offline:

recs <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "gbif_oecophylla_png.csv", package = "tidymapr"))
nrow(recs)
#> [1] 96

# Add three typical mistakes to see how they are caught
bad <- recs[1:3, ]
bad$lon <- c(0, 147.18, -6.6)
bad$lat <- c(0, -9.44, -6.6)     # zeros; Port Moresby (the capital); equal coordinates
both <- rbind(recs, bad)

flags <- geo_clean(both, lon = lon, lat = lat, species = species, value = "flagged")
flags |>
  filter(.summary) |>
  select(lon, lat, .zer, .equ, .cap, .summary)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>     lon   lat .zer  .equ  .cap  .summary
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>   
#> 1   0    0    TRUE  TRUE  FALSE TRUE    
#> 2 147.  -9.44 FALSE FALSE TRUE  TRUE    
#> 3  -6.6 -6.6  FALSE TRUE  FALSE TRUE
clean <- geo_clean(both, lon = lon, lat = lat, species = species)
nrow(clean)
#> [1] 96

How to read it. Each .xxx column is one test, and TRUE means the record was flagged by it; .summary is TRUE if any test flagged the record. (CoordinateCleaner uses the opposite convention, TRUE = passed.) The three added records are flagged: zero coordinates (which are also equal coordinates, so two tests catch them), the capital, and equal coordinates. All 96 real records pass every test, so clean keeps exactly those. Always look at what was removed: a record near a capital may be real, and automated tests are a first filter, not a substitute for knowing the species.

3. Interactive web maps

The concept

A static map is for print; an interactive web map lets readers zoom, switch layers and click features for details. geo_webmap() turns any tidymapr map into a single, self-contained HTML file that opens in any browser, with no server needed: e-mail it, put it on a website, or attach it to a report.

recs_sf <- geo_as_sf(recs, lon, lat)
web <- geo_map(title = "Weaver ant records in Papua New Guinea (GBIF)") |>
  map_points(recs_sf, preset = "occurrence", label = "Records")
dir.create("guide-08-data-webmaps-recipes_files", showWarnings = FALSE)
geo_webmap(web, file = "guide-08-data-webmaps-recipes_files/oecophylla.html", popup = c("year", "basis_of_record"))

Click a point for its year and type of record; switch basemaps at the top right. The same legend and colours as the static map are used, so the two can be published side by side.

4. GeoSpaX recipes

The concept

A recipe is a complete analysis written as a short YAML file: inputs, a list of steps, and outputs. GeoSpaX, the desktop GIS, runs recipes from its menus; tidymapr runs the same files in R. A colleague can therefore repeat your analysis by clicking, and you can re-run theirs in a script, with identical results. Recipes also document methods: the file is the methods section.

rec <- geo_recipe_read(system.file("recipes/points-to-hotspots.yaml", package = "tidymapr"))
rec
#> GeoSpaX recipe "points-to-hotspots" (v1): Incidents → hot spot map (Getis-Ord
#> Gi*)
#> Inputs: layer and field
#> Steps: incidents (io.open), hot (stats.hotspots), style (automap.style), map
#> (export.map), and report (export.report)
#> Outputs: hot, map, and report
geo_recipe_validate(rec)       # an empty table means the recipe is valid
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # ℹ 3 variables: severity <chr>, step <chr>, problem <chr>

Run it on the Meuse soil samples (Chapter 3):

meuse <- terra::unwrap(readRDS(system.file("ex/meuse.rds", package = "terra")))
samples <- sf::st_as_sf(as.data.frame(meuse), coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 28992)
out <- geo_recipe_run(rec, inputs = list(layer = samples, field = "zinc"),
  dir = tempfile(), quiet = TRUE)
out$log
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   step      use            status seconds
#>   <chr>     <chr>          <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 incidents io.open        done      0   
#> 2 hot       stats.hotspots done      0.04
#> 3 style     automap.style  done      0   
#> 4 map       export.map     done      2.16
#> 5 report    export.report  done      0

How to read it. The log lists each step, the GeoSpaX tool it used (use) and whether it finished. out$hot holds the hot-spot results, out$map the map and out$report an HTML report. To write your own recipe, build it with geo_recipe() and recipe_step(), then save it with geo_recipe_write() and open it in GeoSpaX.

References

Zizka, A. et al. (2019). CoordinateCleaner: standardized cleaning of occurrence records from biological collection databases. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 10, 744-751.

GBIF.org. Occurrence records of Oecophylla smaragdina in Papua New Guinea, retrieved through the GBIF API; each record keeps its dataset key and licence (all CC BY 4.0 or CC0).
